result:
The paper's value for an engineer is the artifact, not the science: a 26-item smell catalog for SKILL.md files, a component taxonomy, and a detector recipe you can copy. The empirical claims are descriptive only.

What you get:

- 26 smells grouped into 10 categories, each an inverted community best practice. Five are static checks (word/char caps on body, name, description; backslash paths; XML in frontmatter description); 21 need an LLM judge.
- A judge design that transfers: per-smell definition, one positive and one negative example, binary yes/no, thinking mode. Scored weighted F1 0.78 (P 0.79, R 0.78) against 53 hand-labeled files using a 4-bit quantized Qwen3.6-27B.
- A 13-higher / 44-lower component taxonomy giving you vocabulary for what SKILL.md sections actually contain, plus prevalence (Task 74%, Introduction 64%, References 57%, everything below Practice under 25%).
- Prevalence results: >99% of 238 skills carry at least one smell, 10.5 on average, Rationalization Loophole in 94%. Smells almost never get removed once introduced.

Why the results don't prove much: the "best practices" come from 29 web sources settled by majority vote, so the smells are folklore formalized, not defects shown to cause failures. The paper measures how common these patterns are, never whether they degrade agent behavior. The sample is 238 popular public marketplace skills, so it says little about private or niche skills, and "large-scale" describes the 133k-skill dump, not the 238 files actually analyzed. Detector accuracy rests on 53 labeled files and one quantized open model.

Read the smell list and the judge setup sections. Skim the taxonomy if you need section vocabulary. Skip the evolution analysis unless you care about how skill repos drift over time.
